passages.happening:
Moses introduces everything that follows, from here to chapter 26. These are the commands that God told him to teach, for Israel to follow in the land across the Jordan (verse 1).

He gives the aim. It is ‘so that you and your children and grandchildren may fear the LORD your God all the days of your lives’ (verse 2). And he gives the promise: “Hear, O Israel, and be careful to observe them, so that you may prosper and multiply greatly in a land flowing with milk and honey” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
At the end of chapter 5 the people asked Moses to listen to God for them. Now he begins to deliver what he heard.

In Hebrew the first verse speaks of the commandment, one commandment, and then of statutes and ordinances, many. The Berean Standard Bible renders all three as plurals. Many interpreters take the single word as a heading for the whole. There is one great commandment, loyalty to the LORD, and the detailed laws spell it out. The next verses will say what that one commandment is.

Moses says he was told ‘to teach’ these things. The Hebrew word is from the same root as the later word for a disciple. Deuteronomy shows Moses above all as a teacher. Its law is something to be learned, and not only obeyed.

‘Fear’ here is not terror. It is reverent loyalty, the settled respect of a people who know who their God is. It is the goal of the teaching, and it is meant to last across three generations: you, your child, and your child's child.

A land ‘flowing with milk and honey’ is a land good for flocks and for fruit. The honey probably includes the thick syrup of dates and figs as well as the honey of bees. The promise goes back to the burning bush, where God first used the phrase to Moses.
passages.later:
God made this promise when he first called Moses: he would bring Israel ‘to a good and spacious land, a land flowing with milk and honey’ (Exodus 3:8).

The book of Proverbs opens with the same fear as its starting point: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (Proverbs 1:7).
passages.asks: Moses' aim reaches to grandchildren. Ask what you hope the children after you will know of God, and what you are doing now that would hand it to them. And ask what you fear most. The thing a person fears most is usually the thing that rules them.

passages.happening:
Moses gives the confession on which the whole book rests. “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One” (verse 4).

From the confession comes the command. “And you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your strength” (verse 5).

Then he says where these words must go. “These words I am commanding you today are to be upon your hearts” (verse 6). From the heart they go to the children and into the whole day: “And you shall teach them diligently to your children and speak of them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road, when you lie down and when you get up” (verse 7). They go onto the body: “Tie them as reminders on your hands and bind them on your foreheads” (verse 8). And they go onto the house and the town: “Write them on the doorposts of your houses and on your gates” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
These verses are called the Shema, from their first Hebrew word, ‘hear’. In Hebrew, to hear is also to heed. The one verb covers listening, paying attention and obeying.

The confession stands at the head of the laws as their foundation. Before Israel is told what to do, it is told who its God is.

Verse 4 is six words in Hebrew, with no verb. Hebrew often leaves out ‘is’, so the words can be grouped in more than one way. The Berean Standard Bible reads, ‘The LORD our God, the LORD is One’. Other translations take the last word as ‘alone’: the LORD is Israel's God, and no other. The first stresses that God is one and has no equal. The second stresses that Israel is to have no other god, which fits the warnings that follow in verses 13 to 15. On either reading the verse says that Israel's God is the only God and that he is wholly theirs.

It was said in a world of many gods. Inscriptions from a site in the northern Sinai, from about 800 BC, show that some Israelites spoke of the LORD in local forms, the LORD of this place and the LORD of that, and even gave him a goddess as a partner. Whatever else the Shema answers, it leaves no room for dividing Israel's loyalty.

The command of verse 5 asks for the whole person. The heart, in Hebrew thought, is not mainly where a person feels. It is where a person thinks, chooses and decides. The soul is the living self, one's very life. The third word, translated ‘strength’, is the ordinary Hebrew word for ‘very’ or ‘much’, used here as a noun. It means everything a person has. Old Jewish teachers took it to include a person's wealth. Three times the verse says ‘with all’. Nothing is left outside.

It can seem odd that love is commanded. In the treaties of the ancient world, to ‘love’ a king meant to be loyal to him and serve him alone. Deuteronomy uses that language, so the love meant here is first a settled loyalty. It does not wait for a feeling. But the book fills the word with warmth. It speaks of God setting his affection on Israel's fathers (10:15). And it grounds Israel's love in God's love, which came first (7:7-8). No treaty did that.

Verses 6 to 9 move outward, from the heart to the town gate. The word ‘teach diligently’ comes from a Hebrew verb that means to sharpen, used elsewhere of swords and arrows. The teaching pictured is deliberate and repeated. The pairs in verse 7, sitting and walking, lying down and getting up, are a Hebrew way of saying all the time and everywhere. The first school of faith is the home, and the lesson goes on in ordinary talk as the day passes.

The gates of verse 9 are the town gates, where the elders met and cases were judged. God's words are to mark the private house and the public square alike.

Jewish tradition has kept these verses for more than two thousand years, and keeps them now. The Shema is recited each evening and each morning, following the words ‘when you lie down and when you get up’. The Mishnah, the collection of Jewish law compiled about AD 200, opens with the rules for reciting it, and calls the reciting of its first paragraph receiving the yoke of the kingdom of heaven. Verses 8 and 9 are kept with tefillin, small leather cases holding handwritten passages, and with the mezuzah, a small case holding these words that is fixed to the doorframe of a home. Tefillin were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, so the practice is older than the time of Jesus. Karaite Jews and many Christian interpreters have read verses 8 and 9 as a picture of keeping God's words always in mind. Both readings agree that faith was meant to fill ordinary life.

The Talmud tells that Rabbi Akiva died under Roman torture, after the revolt of AD 132 to 135, reciting the Shema and drawing out its last word, ‘one’, until he died. A Christian who reads these verses is reading words that Jewish men and women have prayed, and have died praying, for a very long time.
passages.later:
The books of Kings use the words of verse 5 for one man only, King Josiah, ‘who turned to the LORD with all his heart and with all his soul and with all his strength’ (2 Kings 23:25).

The book of Proverbs uses the same picture for a parent's teaching: “bind them around your neck, write them on the tablet of your heart” (Proverbs 3:3).

A scribe asked Jesus which commandment is the most important. Jesus answered with the Shema: ‘Hear O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One. Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength’ (Mark 12:29-30). He joined to it the command from Leviticus to love one's neighbor, and said, “All the Law and the Prophets hang on these two commandments” (Matthew 22:40). Jesus did not replace the Shema. He put it at the center.

Paul takes up its words when he writes to the church at Corinth: ‘there is but one God, the Father’ and ‘there is but one Lord, Jesus Christ’ (1 Corinthians 8:6).

James warns that the confession alone is not enough: “You believe that God is one. Good for you! Even the demons believe that” (James 2:19).
passages.hard:
The Shema says that the LORD is one. How then can Christians say that God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit?

The objection is old and serious, and it should be heard in its own terms. Jewish interpreters have heard the Shema as ruling out any plurality in God. The great medieval teacher Maimonides made the unity of God, a oneness unlike any other, one of his thirteen principles of the Jewish faith. Jewish teachers in the Middle Ages pressed this verse against Christian teaching. Islam makes a similar claim about the oneness of God. On this view, to confess Jesus as divine is to add a second god.

Christians have answered in several ways.

The first answer is from history. The earliest Christians were Jews who went on reciting the Shema. They did not think they had left it. Scholars such as Larry Hurtado and Richard Bauckham have argued that when Paul writes of ‘one God, the Father’ and ‘one Lord, Jesus Christ’, he is placing Jesus inside the Shema's own words, within the identity of the one God, and not beside him as a second.

The second answer is from the creeds. The creeds of Nicaea in 325 and Constantinople in 381 begin by confessing one God. The teaching of the Trinity was framed to keep the Shema while confessing what the church believed about the Son and the Spirit. Christians do not confess three gods. They confess the one God, who is Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

A third answer has sometimes been drawn from the Hebrew words of the verse. Some Christian writers have argued that the word for ‘one’ hints at a unity of more than one, because the same word is used of the ‘one flesh’ of marriage. Many Christian scholars think that argument is weak. It is the ordinary Hebrew word for the number one. They prefer to rest the teaching on the New Testament.

The church confesses the Trinity as part of the core of its faith. The disagreement with Jewish readers and with Muslim readers is real, and it should be stated honestly. The Shema alone does not settle it for either side. What Christians and Jews share here is not small: there is one God, he is to be loved with everything, and nothing else may be put in his place.
passages.asks: The Shema asks for all the heart, all the soul and all the strength. Ask which part of your life you have quietly kept back: your thinking, your safety, or your money. And follow the words outward as Moses does. Ask whether they are in your talk at home, in your work, and at your door, or only in the place where you worship.

passages.t: When you are full: do not forget, and do not test
passages.happening:
Moses looks ahead to a good day and sees a danger in it. God will bring Israel into a land with cities ‘that you did not build’, houses full of good things, wells ‘that you did not dig’, and vineyards and olive groves ‘that you did not plant’ (verses 10-11). When they have eaten and are full, “be careful not to forget the LORD who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (verse 12).

Then three commands. “Fear the LORD your God, serve Him only, and take your oaths in His name” (verse 13). Israel must not follow the gods of the peoples around it, for God, who lives among them, ‘is a jealous God’ (verses 14-15).

“Do not test the LORD your God as you tested Him at Massah” (verse 16). They are to keep his commands and ‘do what is right and good in the sight of the LORD’ (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
The warning is one long sentence in Hebrew. It piles up the gifts first, cities, houses, wells, vines and olive trees, and only then reaches its point. The hearer feels the weight of what is given before hearing the danger.

Every item on the list is something that takes years. The hill country of Canaan had few springs, and people lived by cutting cisterns into the rock to hold the winter rain. Olive trees take years to bear. To receive all of this at once was to receive the work of other people's lifetimes.

The danger Moses names is not hunger. It is a full stomach. In Hebrew, to forget is less a slip of memory than a failure of loyalty. Israel will not decide one day to leave the LORD. It will simply stop remembering him while it enjoys what he gave.

The three commands of verse 13 cover the inner life, the outward practice and the public word. In the ancient world a person swore by the god he trusted to punish a lie. To swear by the LORD alone was to name him alone as the judge of one's word. The Hebrew puts ‘him’ first for stress, which is why the translation can say ‘serve Him only’.

Massah means ‘testing’. It was the place, told in Exodus 17, where the people had no water and demanded that God prove himself, saying, ‘Is the LORD among us or not?’ The Hebrew has a play on words: do not test him as you tested him at Testing. To test God in this sense is to make trust depend on proof. It sets the terms that God must meet before he will be believed. That is a different thing from an honest question, which the Bible allows.
passages.later:
Exodus tells what happened at Massah: “He named the place Massah and Meribah because the Israelites quarreled, and because they tested the LORD” (Exodus 17:7).

Jesus answered the devil from this passage twice. When the devil took him to the top of the temple and told him to throw himself down, since God had promised to guard him, Jesus answered, ‘Do not put the Lord your God to the test’ (Matthew 4:7). He would not force his Father to prove his care. When the devil offered him all the kingdoms of the world in return for worship, Jesus quoted verse 13: ‘Worship the Lord your God and serve Him only’ (Matthew 4:10).

His first answer came from chapter 8 of this book. All three were taken from Moses' preaching on the wilderness years. Israel was tested there for forty years and failed at Massah. Jesus was tested there for forty days and kept faith. The Gospels themselves draw this line.
passages.asks: Moses says the risk comes ‘when you eat and are satisfied’. Ask whether you pray less when life is going well, and what that shows. And ask whether you have ever set God a test, asking him to prove himself before you would trust him. Notice that Jesus, with every reason to ask for a sign, refused to demand one.

passages.happening:
Moses pictures a day in the future. A child asks a parent, ‘What is the meaning of the decrees and statutes and ordinances that the LORD our God has commanded you?’ (verse 20).

The parent is given the answer. ‘We were slaves of Pharaoh in Egypt, but the LORD brought us out of Egypt with a mighty hand’ (verse 21). God did great signs against Pharaoh before their eyes (verse 22). “But He brought us out from there to lead us in and give us the land that He had sworn to our fathers” (verse 23). And he gave these statutes for their good, ‘that we may always be prosperous and preserved’ (verse 24).

The answer ends: “And if we are careful to observe every one of these commandments before the LORD our God, as He has commanded us, then that will be our righteousness” (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
The chapter closes with a small lesson for the home, a question and an answer. The question assumes that the child has seen the laws being kept, at the table, in the calendar and at the door, and wants to know why.

The text expects children to ask. It wants their questions answered and not hushed.

Look at how the answer begins. The child asks about rules. The parent does not begin with rules. The parent begins with a story: slavery, rescue, and a promised land. The laws make sense only inside that story. They are how a rescued people lives.

The parent says ‘we’. ‘We were slaves.’ Neither the parent nor the child was in Egypt. The parent speaks as one who belongs to the people it happened to, and draws the child in. Israel confessed its faith by telling what God had done.

This question and answer live on in Jewish homes. The text read at the Passover meal, the Haggadah, takes the question of its ‘wise son’ from verse 20, and answers the children with the words of verse 21, ‘We were slaves’.

Verse 24 says why the laws were given: so that the people might do well and be kept alive. God's commands are part of his kindness.
passages.later:
Exodus gives the same pattern for the Passover: ‘In the future, when your son asks you, “What does this mean?” you are to tell him, “With a mighty hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery”’ (Exodus 13:14).

Joshua set up twelve stones at the Jordan so that children would ask about them too: ‘In the future, when your children ask, “What do these stones mean to you?”’ (Joshua 4:6).

Paul tells Christian parents to do what this passage asks: “Fathers, do not provoke your children to wrath; instead, bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (Ephesians 6:4).
passages.hard:
Verse 25 says that keeping the commands ‘will be our righteousness’. Does that mean a person is made right with God by obeying?

Read by itself, the verse can sound like a way of earning God's favor, and some readers have heard it so. Some Protestant readers take verses like this as the law's offer of life on condition of full obedience, which sinful people cannot meet. They point to Paul, who writes that ‘no one will be justified in His sight by works of the law’ (Romans 3:20).

Other readers stress the setting. The parent's answer begins with rescue and not with effort: ‘We were slaves of Pharaoh in Egypt, but the LORD brought us out.’ In Deuteronomy the word ‘righteousness’ names faithful conduct inside a covenant that God has already made. In 24:13, returning a poor man's cloak ‘will be credited to you as righteousness before the LORD your God’. Jewish interpreters have long read the Torah as a gracious gift to a people already chosen. The scholar E. P. Sanders, in 1977, described the pattern this way: a person enters the covenant by God's grace and stays in it by obedience, with a way of atonement provided for failure. Lutheran and Reformed interpreters have replied that Paul still sets human doing against God's gift.

Christians read the relation between Deuteronomy and Paul in different ways, and these notes take no side. All of these readings agree on one thing. In Deuteronomy grace comes before obedience, not after it. And Paul himself quotes chapter 30 of this book to describe the righteousness that comes by faith (Romans 10:6-8).
passages.asks: When the child asks why, the parent tells what God has done. Ask whether you could give that answer: what God has brought you out of, and what he has brought you into. And if a child or a new believer asked you why you live as you do, ask whether your first words would be about rules or about rescue.
